# What Is a Quarterly Business Review (QBR)?

Source: https://lowob.com/research/what-is-a-quarterly-business-review/
Publisher: lowob (https://lowob.com)
Published: 2026-11-17
Function: Revenue

> Summary: A quarterly business review (QBR) is a meeting held every three months in which a supplier and a customer review results against the goals they agreed, discuss what has changed in the customer's business and set goals for the next quarter. Its purpose is to keep both sides agreed on the value being delivered, well before a renewal date. A QBR that only presents usage statistics is a report, not a review. The test is whether the customer leaves with decisions and owners.

*Figure: Where this piece sits: the commercial line, where the build starts.*

## Key points

- Gainsight, a customer success software vendor, describes a QBR as a strategic meeting held once every three months to show business impact and agree next steps, ideally in under an hour.
- Gainsight distinguishes the executive business review (EBR), built for senior audiences and focused on business outcomes, held every six months for strategic accounts.
- In Gartner's 2023 survey of 1,503 respondents, 60% of technology buyers involved in renewal or expansion decisions said they regret nearly every purchase they make.
- A Gartner survey of 243 sales leaders in 2025 found 73% of chief sales officers focused on growing revenue from existing customers.
- Each QBR produces commercial decisions: goals, owners and dates. Recording them, and grading them at the next review, is what turns the meeting into evidence for renewal.

## What a quarterly business review means

A QBR is part of account management, not support. It sits between day-to-day contact and the renewal conversation. Gainsight's guide lists five core elements: a review of performance against agreed goals using data, a discussion of the customer's challenges and changes, joint goal-setting for the next quarter, a demonstration of value including return on investment, and next steps with owners and timelines.

The term is used loosely. Three related meetings are often confused.

| Meeting | Who attends (customer side) | Focus | Typical frequency |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| QBR | Managers, team leads and active users | Progress against goals, usage, issues, next quarter's goals | Every three months |
| Executive business review (EBR) | C-suite, vice presidents and directors | Business outcomes and strategic value | Every six months for strategic accounts; yearly for growth accounts (Gainsight) |
| Renewal value review | Sponsor and decision makers | What the term achieved and what the next term should deliver | Once, about 120 days before renewal in **lowob**'s calendar |

For new customers, Gainsight suggests the first EBR after initial value is realised, typically three to six months after implementation. Not every account needs a quarterly meeting; smaller accounts can get a lighter digital review.

## Why it matters for a commercial team

### Buyers often regret what they bought

Gartner's 2023 survey, run from February to March across North America, Western Europe and Asia/Pacific, found 60% of technology buyers involved in renewal or expansion decisions regret nearly every purchase. Gartner attributes most of that regret to dysfunction inside distributed buying teams, not to the supplier or the product. Its recommendations include training customer-facing teams to spot regret signals, such as buyers revisiting decisions or internal conflict, and giving buying teams shared spaces to review objectives and build business cases.

A QBR is the natural place to do both, while there is still time to act.

### Growth is expected from the existing base

Gartner's 2025 survey of chief sales officers found 73% focused on growing revenue from existing customers, and 57% ranked retention and growth among their top three priorities. [Renewals and Expansion](https://lowob.com/research/renewals-and-expansion/) sets out why: for most mid-size B2B firms the existing base barely grows on its own. QBRs are where the evidence for an expansion is built, in the customer's terms.

> A QBR that shows usage charts is a report. A QBR that ends with agreed goals, owners and dates is a review.

## How to run one

| Section | What to bring | What to leave with |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Goals from last quarter | The goals agreed at the last review, with results | Each goal marked met, missed or changed, with the reason |
| Customer changes | Questions about strategy, people and budget | Updated sponsor and stakeholder list |
| Value delivered | Outcomes in the customer's measures, not product metrics | An agreed statement of value for the quarter |
| Issues | Open support cases and risks | Owners and dates for each |
| Next quarter | Proposed goals | Two or three goals the customer has agreed |
| Next steps | A draft action list | Actions with owners on both sides |

Three habits separate useful QBRs from routine ones. Send a short pre-read so the meeting is spent on decisions. Let the customer present part of it, so the value statement is theirs. Keep it to an hour, as Gainsight advises.

In **lowob**'s model, the goals agreed at a QBR are decisions with a reason, an owner, a status and an expected outcome. The next QBR is the natural point for [outcome write-back](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-outcome-write-back/): each goal is graded against what happened. Over a year, that record becomes the renewal case, and it feeds the [customer health score](https://lowob.com/research/what-is-customer-health-scoring/) with evidence rather than impressions. An agent can draft the pre-read from CRM, usage and support data at autonomy level 1. A person checks and presents it, and nothing goes to the customer without that review.

## lowob takeaways

- **A QBR is a review, not a report.** It should end with agreed goals, owners and dates.
- **It is an early warning system.** Sponsor changes and internal conflict surface here before renewal.
- **Match the meeting to the account.** QBRs for the top tier, EBRs for executives, lighter reviews for the rest.
- **Grade last quarter's goals.** The written record of goals and results becomes the renewal case.

## Common questions

### What should be included in a quarterly business review?

Results against last quarter's goals, changes in the customer's business, the value delivered in the customer's terms, open issues, and agreed goals and actions for the next quarter.

### What is the difference between a QBR and an EBR?

A QBR reviews progress and usage with managers and users every quarter. An executive business review covers business outcomes with senior leaders, usually every six or twelve months.

### How long should a QBR be?

Gainsight recommends no more than an hour. A pre-read sent in advance keeps the meeting on decisions rather than presentation.

### Do all customers need a QBR?

No. Most firms run them for their largest or most strategic accounts and use lighter, often digital, reviews for smaller ones.

Pull the notes from your last three QBRs with your largest account and list every goal agreed in them. If you cannot say which were met, start the next QBR by grading them with the customer.
